lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Verify that the code URL is a real, accessible portfolio or repository.
items.because: If it is a GitHub profile, a direct URL to polished, relevant repositories would be clearer.

items.says: Consider adding a LinkedIn profile if it is complete and consistent with the résumé.
State the expected degree more formally if useful for the target role.
items.because: The current “Ph.D. candidate” label is generic.

items.says: Consider adding a relevant dissertation topic, advisor, research area, qualification, honor, or publication.
items.because: Relevant specifics may be more valuable than the generic candidate label.

items.says: Make date formatting consistent across entries.
items.because: The résumé should use one dash style and month format throughout.

items.says: Consider adding GPA or honors only if they are strong and useful.
items.because: Coursework is probably unnecessary at this experience level.

items.says: Clarify whether you supervised six employees or six people worked opening shifts.
items.because: The current wording is ambiguous.

items.says: Give the budget or operation’s scale if meaningful.
items.because: “Within budget” is a weak outcome without context.

items.says: Use a spelling convention suited to the target employers consistently.
items.because: For U.S. employers, “labor” may be more natural than “labour.”

items.says: Keep the bakery management detail brief.
items.because: It is not directly relevant to quantitative research, and one strong bullet may suffice.

items.says: Clarify the period or comparison basis for the unsold-bread percentages.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether they cover a week, month, or season.

items.says: Explain what operational change you made.
items.because: The bullet says the percentage fell but does not clearly show what changed because of your work.

items.says: Verify the denominator for the unsold-bread metric.
items.because: It must be a percentage of production rather than sales or inventory to support the wording.

items.says: Explain whether the signal was added to the desk book or evaluated alone.
items.because: “Raised the desk book’s Sharpe ratio” implies attribution that may be difficult to establish.

items.says: Give the universe or number of contracts if space permits.
items.because: The result needs more methodological context.

items.says: Confirm that the 18 months were genuinely out of sample.
items.because: Parameter selection or model changes during that period would undermine the description.

items.says: Clarify that the Sharpe ratios are annualized consistently and use the same return series.
items.because: The comparison will attract scrutiny.

items.says: State what “keeping 90% of gross returns” measures.
items.because: It could mean original gross P&L, return, or alpha.

items.says: Tie the slippage estimate to the first bullet’s test period and cost model.
items.because: The measurement bases need to be explicit.

items.says: Clarify the percentages’ denominators and comparison points.
items.because: Several related percentages are difficult to interpret without them.

items.says: Clarify how gross returns and slippage relate.
items.because: Mixing those measures can make the result difficult to interpret.

items.says: Specify whether the tests concerned forecast loss, predictive accuracy, or return performance.
items.because: The bullet does not say what was tested.

items.says: Replace the imprecise phrase “forecast gain.”
items.because: It should distinguish predictive accuracy from trading performance.

items.says: Give a significance level, number of significant series, or another test result.
items.because: Saying the tests were used does not tell the reader what they showed.

items.says: Check whether “nested” describes the baseline and whether the test handled nesting correctly.
items.because: Standard Diebold–Mariano testing can require care with nested models.

items.says: The opening participial phrase does not attach correctly to the subject.
items.because: It creates a grammatical problem in the feature-store bullet.

items.says: Make “Joining” unambiguous.
items.because: It could describe combining data or be a mistaken tense choice.

items.says: Specify what was aligned or joined point-in-time.
items.because: It could refer to the features, raw data, or both.

items.says: Consider separating the feature-store contributions.
items.because: The bullet combines alignment, late-print handling, schema versioning, and store development.

items.says: Quantify the feature store’s scale if possible.
items.because: Data volume, latency, instruments, or reduced debugging time would show its scope.

items.says: Explain the value of its reuse in two later projects.
items.because: The reuse shows adoption but not what it achieved.

items.says: Annualizing a daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying by 252 is incorrect.
items.because: It is generally multiplied by the square root of the number of periods, and the mistake could undermine confidence in the quantitative work.

items.says: Use a stronger measure of documentation adoption if available.
items.because: The first-week onboarding claim is slightly informal and difficult to verify.

items.says: Specify whether the documentation covered key backtest risks.
items.because: Data leakage, universe selection, execution, missing data, and parameter selection matter beyond general assumptions.

items.says: Place this supporting bullet after the core modeling results.
items.because: The research results should lead the internship entry.

items.says: Add relevant pipeline tools or technologies if they are not clear elsewhere.
Qualify “every run reproducible” if the pipeline did not control all relevant inputs.
items.because: The claim requires control of seeds, configurations, software versions, and data inputs.

items.says: Consider naming the parallelization or cluster environment.
items.because: Production-scale computation may matter to target roles.

items.says: Remove the first-person phrasing “my proof.”
items.because: The contribution should sound professional and precise.

items.says: Verify the journal name and “under review” status.
items.because: That status is appropriate only if the paper was submitted and is currently under review.

items.says: Make the log-factor result accurate and understandable.
items.because: It may be unclear to non-specialists.

items.says: Clarify authorship if the paper is collaborative.
items.because: The wording should not imply sole authorship.

items.says: Consider a publications or working-papers section for the JASA paper.
items.because: It may be important to the candidacy.

items.says: Keep the teaching bullet only if it serves the target role.
items.because: It matters less to research-focused roles than the simulation and theory work.

items.says: Clarify what the count of 60 students represents.
items.because: It could be course enrollment or recitation attendance.

items.says: Verify the basis of the 4.8/5 teaching rating.
items.because: It should be institutionally recognized and based on a meaningful number of responses.

items.says: Separate the R-package achievement from unrelated lab responsibilities.
items.because: The bullet is overloaded with software, systems administration, service, and grading.

items.says: Resolve what “which was downloaded 3,000 times” refers to.
items.because: The grammar makes the package, grading, or entire set of activities possible antecedents.

items.says: Verify the source and meaning of the download count.
items.because: It should reflect actual package downloads, not page views or repository clones.

items.says: Add evidence of package quality or adoption if available.
items.because: Documentation, tests, external users, citations, or maintenance would strengthen it.

items.says: Give cluster maintenance a measurable result or technical scope if retained.
items.because: It needs that context to justify space.

items.says: Clarify whether this study is independent of the Northpeak work.
items.because: The shared HAR-RV and volatility-forecasting claims may look like double-counting.

items.says: Describe the forecast evaluation design.
items.because: Windows, forecast horizon, and test-period-free hyperparameter selection would establish credibility.

items.says: Clarify that the 7% is a relative QLIKE reduction.
items.because: It should not be mistaken for a seven-percentage-point change.

items.says: Calling the drop from 0.20 to 0.15 a 33% improvement is arithmetically wrong.
items.because: It is a 25% reduction.

items.says: Name the forecast-error metric.
items.because: “Forecast error” is too generic.

items.says: Remove this result if it describes the same experiment as the previous bullet.
items.because: It may duplicate the more informative QLIKE result.

items.says: Support the attribution to both new features and asymmetric loss with an ablation or comparison.
items.because: Otherwise the bullet implies more causal attribution than the experiment establishes.

items.says: A change from 52% to 58% is not a 6% relative increase.
items.because: It is six percentage points, or about an 11.5% relative increase.

items.says: Avoid repeating the model and 30-index universe.
items.because: Both already appear in the project’s first bullet.

items.says: Give an appropriate trading or statistical baseline for directional hit rate.
items.because: Directional accuracy can mislead when forecasts are near zero or classes are imbalanced.

items.says: Consider whether directional hit rate is relevant to the target role.
items.because: QLIKE and calibration may be more persuasive for volatility modeling.

items.says: Reduce the Volatility Forecasting Study’s three overlapping result bullets to distinct contributions.
items.because: Each metric should add information rather than repeat largely the same model result.

items.says: Remove the redundant “top 2%” phrasing if space is tight.
items.because: “41st of 2,900” already communicates the rank.

items.says: Clarify your individual contribution to the team result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether you built the ensemble, engineered features, or contributed elsewhere.

items.says: Reword “cut validation leakage” more carefully.
items.because: The new folds likely reduced leakage or improved validation validity, but did not necessarily quantify leakage.

items.says: Explain how the 0.02 score gap closed.
items.because: The local score may have decreased, the leaderboard score increased, or both.

items.says: State the direction of the local-versus-leaderboard gap.
items.because: A gap can be measured either way.

items.says: Make the progression from 900 candidates to 300 final features easy to follow.
items.because: The earlier competition bullet mentions only the 300 engineered features.

items.says: Confirm that the unchanged validation score used the corrected time-grouped folds.
items.because: A leaky split would not support the result.

items.says: Make your individual ownership of the team contribution clear.
The “Programming” label misclassifies PyTorch and Kafka as languages.
items.because: PyTorch is a machine-learning framework and Kafka is a distributed messaging platform.

items.says: Connect Kafka to a real project or remove it.
items.because: It appears nowhere in the experience bullets.

items.says: Add other relevant tools only if you have meaningful experience with them.
“Econometircs” is misspelled.
items.because: The correct spelling is “econometrics.”

items.says: Make the methods more parallel and specific.
items.because: “High-dimensional statistics” is broad, while “gradient boosting” is a modeling method alongside broader fields.

items.says: List additional methods only when the experience section substantiates them.
items.because: The skills section should not introduce unevidenced methods.
